case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) trying to make a clinical decision about the given patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Current Context]
- You have examined the patient case.
- Form your own clinical judgment.

[Task]
Based on the case below, state your initial decision and reasoning.

- Keep your response under 5 sentences.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Clinician's current statement]
Given the patient's history of travel to Mexico, presentation of symptoms, and the presence of multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications on CT, I believe the most appropriate next step in management is option B: serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites. Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {
    "mental_demand": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. Upon further questioning, she reported travel to Mexico in the last year. She denied eating undercooked meat, living in the Ohio River Valley, recent insect bites, exposure to cats, puppies, or lactating female dogs, or receiving immunocompromising or immunomodulating therapy.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's history of travel to Mexico, presentation of symptoms, and the presence of multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications on CT, I believe the most appropriate next step in management is option B: serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and inspection of stool for ova and parasites. This patient's clinical picture is suggestive of neurocysticercosis, and further testing is necessary to confirm the diagnosis before initiating specific treatment.

You are right to suspect neurocysticercosis given the calcifications and travel history. However, with active symptoms and CSF findings of neutrophilic pleocytosis, we should also consider other causes like neurocysticercosis in the acute inflammatory phase or other CNS infections. A lumbar puncture has been done, but did we send the CSF for specific parasitic studies beyond the cysticercus IgG?

While I acknowledge the importance of considering other CNS infections given the neutrophilic pleocytosis, the patient's travel history and imaging findings strongly point towards neurocysticercosis. Option B remains the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis through serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and stool examination. Once we have definitive information, we can then tailor the treatment more effectively.

That's a sound approach to pursue definitive confirmation. The serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies, particularly Taenia solium antibodies in serum or CSF, and stool O&P are indeed key steps to confirm neurocysticercosis. However, given the active CSF findings, we must also consider that a positive result would require immediate initiation of antiparasitic therapy, not just further testing.

[Clinician's current statement]
I appreciate your emphasis on the urgency given the CSF findings, but I still maintain that confirming the diagnosis through serologic testing for antihelminth antibodies and stool examination is crucial before we initiate any specific treatment. Once we have a definitive diagnosis, we can promptly address the active infection appropriately.

Respond directly to this statement.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

[Role]

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.

[Cognitive Burden]

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.9. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).

case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old female patient with type 2 diabetes presented to an emergency department with 3 days of syncope, headache, fatigue, myalgias, fevers, chills, nausea, and vomiting. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the head (Figure 1) showed multiple coarse, dystrophic calcifications. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with contrast showed no active lesions. She was admitted and treated empirically for sepsis. Urinalysis, chest radiography, CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, antinuclear antibody screen, HIV antibodies, cysticercus immunoglobulin G (IgG), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coccidioides antibody, and blood and CSF culture results were unremarkable. CSF analysis showed the following counts: protein, 0.095 g/dL (to convert protein to g/L, multiply by 10); glucose, 92 mg/dL (to convert glucose to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); white blood cells, 148/µL (to convert white blood cell count to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001); red blood cells, 0.000036 × 106/µL (to convert red blood cell count to × 1012/L, multiply by 1); neutrophils, 81% (to convert neutrophils to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01); and monocytes, 19% (to convert monocytes to a proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01). One week following admission, the patient reported floaters in her right eye with normal vision. Ophthalmoscopic examination showed moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy and scattered and linear formations of chorioretinal lesions with mild patchy venular staining, but no substantial leakage was observed on fluorescein angiography (FA) (Figure 1). Mild vitritis was observed in both eyes. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans of the lesions nasal to the optic nerve in the left eye (Figure 1) showed retinal atrophy, retinal pigment epithelium hypertrophy, and choroidal hyperreflectivity. case_info.explanation: West Nile virus (WNV) chorioretinitis D. Serologic testing for antiviral antibodies Recent encephalitis and radial chorioretinal lesions without leakage on FA are consistent with WNV. WNV IgG and IgM tests were positive. Rheumatoid factor, which can cause false-positive WNV serology, was negative. The differential diagnosis for multifocal chorioretinitis includes nonhelminthic infectious causes, such as presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS), and infectious causes, such as syphilis, tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, pneumocystis choroiditis, and WNV. Although vitritis makes POHS much less likely, 5% of POHS patients, as a subset of multifocal choroiditis, have a linear streak of histoplasmosis spots parallel to the equator (ie, Schlaegel lines). Ocular toxoplasmosis classically presents with vitritis overlying focal retinitis (ie, a headlight in the fog). Active toxoplasmosis is unlikely without retinitis (choice A). The remaining etiologies are unlikely with negative serology and inconsistent imaging. Helminthic infections can cause chorioretinitis. However, typically there are also anterior segment findings, like keratitis or iridocyclitis in onchocerciasis. Ocular cysticercosis can cause intracranial calcifications. Toxocara and other nematodes can cause subretinal tracks with diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), consistent with linear chorioretinal lesions. However, serologic and stool studies and peripheral blood smears are of little utility in helminthic infections (choice B).1Stool ova and parasite testing is low yield for toxocara, because ingested eggs cause an eosinophilic granulomatous immune reaction incompatible with helminth survival.2Although multiple toxocariasis phenotypes have been described, including DUSN and diffuse chorioretinal inflammation, the most common presentation is unilateral pediatric subretinal peripheral or posterior pole granulomas with clear media. Adult ocular toxocariasis is exceedingly rare and usually presents with vitritis overlying a hazy white granuloma.3 Noninfectious causes include sarcoidosis, punctate inner choroidopathy, birdshot retinochoroidopathy, idiopathic multifocal choroiditis, and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis. Linear periphlebitis and inflammatory aggregates in the vitreous, described as a string of pearls, can be seen in sarcoidosis. The other autoimmune etiologies are diagnoses of exclusion. Infection should be ruled out before treating empirically with corticosteroids (choice C). WNV, detected with serologic testing for antiviral antibodies (choice D), is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted byCulexgenus mosquitoes. Approximately 70% to 80% of human WNV infections are subclinical. Most symptomatic cases present with acute fever, headache, weakness, myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, and/or transient maculopapular rash. Less than 1% of cases exhibit neuroinvasive disease. The most common ocular complication is multifocal chorioretinitis, but cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, optic neuritis, retinal vasculitis, and anterior uveitis have been reported. Age greater than 45 years and diabetes are risk factors for WNV chorioretinitis.4 In neuroinvasive disease, CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, neutrophils predominate early, are rapidly recruited to the site of WNV infection in mice, and support viral replication.5 MRI may show abnormalities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, and brainstem in patients with encephalitis. Fundus photos and retina OCT typically show a linear chorioretinitis due to spread along the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL).6WNV can spread hematogenously via the choroid or neurally from the central nervous system to the RNFL, which may explain the combination of scattered and linear lesion formations in this patient. The patient’s symptoms and vitritis resolved with observation, while chorioretinal lesions persisted (Figure 2).
